knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = NA, fig.align = "center")

## Introduction

This micro case illustrates the consequences of using weak instruments
in instrumental variables estimation.

While instrumental variables can correct for endogeneity,
their performance critically depends on the strength of the first stage.

## Data Generating Process

In this simulation, treatment is endogenous, but the instrument is only
weakly correlated with treatment assignment.

```{r dgp}
set.seed(123)

n <- 2000

# Unobserved ability
ability <- rnorm(n)

# Weak instrument
z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)

# Treatment: weak dependence on z
treat <- 0.3 * z + 0.7 * ability + rnorm(n)
treat <- as.integer(treat > median(treat))

# Potential outcomes
y0 <- 10 + ability + rnorm(n)
y1 <- y0 + 2

# Observed outcome
y <- y0 + treat * (y1 - y0)

case3B <- data.frame(y, treat, z, ability, y0, y1)
```

## OLS Benchmark

```{r ols}
ols <- lm(y ~ treat, data = case3B)
summary(ols)
```

## Weak First Stage

```{r first-stage}
fs <- lm(treat ~ z, data = case3B)
summary(fs)
```

## IV with Weak Instrument

We now estimate the causal effect using instrumental variables.
Because the model is just-identified, the IV estimator is equivalent
to the Wald estimator.

```{r iv-wald}
# Wald estimator
wald <- cov(case3B$y, case3B$z) / cov(case3B$treat, case3B$z)
wald
```

```{r iv-2sls}
# Two-stage least squares
library(AER)
iv_2sls <- ivreg(y ~ treat | z, data = case3B)
summary(iv_2sls)
```

## Variance Explosion with Weak Instruments

Although the IV estimator is consistent, weak instruments can lead to
extreme variability in finite samples. To illustrate this, we repeat
the experiment many times and examine the distribution of the IV
estimator.

```{r iv-variance}
set.seed(123)

B <- 500
iv_estimates <- numeric(B)

for (b in 1:B) {

  ability <- rnorm(n)
  z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)

  treat <- 0.3 * z + 0.7 * ability + rnorm(n)
  treat <- as.integer(treat > median(treat))

  y0 <- 10 + ability + rnorm(n)
  y1 <- y0 + 2
  y <- y0 + treat * (y1 - y0)

  iv_estimates[b] <- cov(y, z) / cov(treat, z)
}

hist(
  iv_estimates,
  breaks = 40,
  col = "lightgray",
  border = "white",
  main = "Weak IV: Variance Explosion",
  xlab = "IV estimates"
)

abline(v = 2, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

## True ATE

```{r true-ate}
mean(case3B$y1 - case3B$y0)
```

## Conclusion

This case demonstrates that weak instruments lead to imprecise
and potentially misleading IV estimates.

When instruments are weak, IV estimators may perform worse than
biased OLS estimators in finite samples.
